etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire, borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (“old”). Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, and sire.

definitions.definition: A man of a higher rank or position.
to a knight or other low member of the peerage.
A respectful term of address to a man of higher rank or position, particularly:

quote.citation: 1991 May 12, “Kidnapped!”, in Jeeves and Wooster, Series 2, Episode 5:
quote.text: Jeeves: Foreign travel often liberates emotions best kept in check, sir. The air of North America is notoriously stimulating in this regard, as witness the regrettable behavior of its inhabitants in 1776.B. Wooster: Hm? What happened in 1776, Jeeves?Jeeves: I prefer not to dwell on it, if it's convenient to you, sir.

definitions.definition: A respectful term of address to an  adult male (often older), especially if his name or proper title is unknown.
(transitive, informal) To address another individual using "sir".

quote.citation: 1997, Ed Solomon, Men in Black, spoken by Agent K (Tommy Lee Jones):
quote.text: Don't "Sir" me, young man, you have no idea who you're dealing with!
